etymology: From English + martyr (Greek martys, a witness); the Protestant believers burned in England, chiefly under Mary Tudor, for the recovered gospel.
biblical_def: The English Martyrs are the Protestant believers who were burned, hanged, or otherwise put to death in England for the recovered gospel, most of them in the brief and bloody reign of Mary Tudor (1553–58), whom history remembers as "Bloody Mary." Some three hundred were burned in less than four years — bishops and plowmen, scholars and women, the famous and the unknown. William Tyndale had already been strangled and burned abroad for giving England the Bible; under Mary the fires came home. Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, and Nicholas Ridley — the Oxford martyrs — were burned for denying the Mass and confessing justification by faith. Latimer comforted Ridley in the flames with words England never forgot: "Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man; we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out." Their stories were gathered by John Foxe in his Acts and Monuments — the "Book of Martyrs" — which next to the Bible shaped English piety for generations. This dictionary honors the English Martyrs as faithful witnesses who counted Christ and His truth dearer than their own lives, fulfilling the Lord's word that the faithful unto death receive the crown of life.
webster_summary: The Protestant believers burned in England for the gospel, chiefly under Mary Tudor ("Bloody Mary," 1553–58) — some three hundred, including the Oxford martyrs Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley. Their witness, gathered in Foxe's Book of Martyrs, shaped English piety for centuries.

corruption_summary: The age that prizes comfort cannot imagine dying for a doctrine, and so it recasts the English Martyrs as victims of political intolerance rather than witnesses to truth; the deeper corruption is to forget that they died for the very gospel a comfortable church now treats as negotiable.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern world reads the English Martyrs through the lens of religious liberty and tolerance, as if their tragedy were merely that people once killed over religion. There is truth in lamenting the cruelty. But to stop there is to miss the point of their death: they did not die for tolerance; they died for justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, and the rejection of the Mass — the gospel itself. They "loved not their lives unto the death" (Rev 12:11) because they loved Christ more.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the historical record, preserved in Foxe. The principle to recover is the costliness of the truth they died for. A church that treats the doctrines of grace and the gospel of faith alone as matters indifferent has forgotten that men were burned to recover them. "Fear not them which kill the body" (Matt 10:28): the English Martyrs feared God more than the fire, and their candle, by God's grace, was never put out.

etymology: From Greek hagnos (pure, chaste), later associated with Latin agnus (lamb); a young Roman virgin martyred under the persecutions of the early fourth century.
biblical_def: Agnes was a young Roman girl, perhaps no more than twelve or thirteen, martyred at Rome in the persecutions of the early fourth century, probably under Diocletian, and remembered ever after as a pattern of purity and courage in the face of death. The ancient accounts, gathered by Ambrose and Prudentius within a century of her death, tell of a child of a Christian family who refused both marriage and the renouncing of Christ, was threatened with shame and with the sword, and went to her death with a calm beyond her years, more afraid of sin than of the executioner. Her name was joined to the Latin word for lamb, agnus, and she became a symbol of the spotless witness who follows the Lamb. The dictionary honors the historical fact: a young believer who would not deny her Lord or surrender her chastity, and who sealed her confession with her blood. It does not honor the later legendary embellishments, nor the cult of relics and the veneration of saints that grew up around her memory in the medieval church — honors that belong to God and His Lamb alone. Agnes stands among the cloud of witnesses who loved not their lives unto the death.
webster_summary: A young Roman girl martyred in the early-fourth-century persecutions, remembered for refusing both marriage and the denial of Christ, and dying with a courage beyond her years. Her name was joined to agnus, "lamb." Honored here for her witness, not for the later cult built around her.

corruption_summary: Agnes is corrupted by the medieval cult that turned a faithful young martyr into an object of veneration, prayer, and relic-devotion — honors due to God alone — and by the modern skeptic who, finding legendary growth in her story, dismisses the historical martyrdom altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption built upon Agnes is the cult of the saints: a real and honorable martyr made into an intercessor to be prayed to, her supposed relics venerated, her memory ringed with legend. The dictionary honors what is honorable — a child who would not deny Christ — while naming the veneration as a corruption of the New Testament priesthood of all believers, in which there is one Mediator (1 Tim 2:5) and one Lamb whom the redeemed follow (Rev 14:4). Honor is due her courage; worship and prayer are due God alone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the relic-cult, but the modern skeptic errs in the other direction, using the later legendary embellishments to deny that any such girl was martyred. The principle to recover is simpler than either error: a young believer once confessed Christ before men (Matt 10:32) and died rather than deny Him or defile her body bought with a price (1 Cor 6:20). Her witness needs no embellishment and no veneration — only to be remembered, and followed, as she followed the Lamb.

etymology: From the Albigenses (named for the town of Albi in southern France) + crusade (Latin crux, cross); the thirteenth-century war Rome waged against the Cathar heretics and the dissenters of Languedoc.
biblical_def: The Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) was the war Pope Innocent III and the French crown waged against the Cathars, or Albigenses, of southern France — a campaign that mingled the suppression of a genuine heresy with appalling cruelty and the crushing of the Languedoc. The Cathars themselves held a dualist heresy, not biblical Christianity at all: two eternal principles of good and evil, the material world the work of an evil god, the body a prison, marriage and procreation suspect, and a secret "perfect" class who alone were saved. This was no recovery of the gospel but an old Manichaean error, and the dictionary does not romanticize it. Yet the crusade against it became a byword for atrocity. At the storming of Béziers in 1209, when asked how to tell Catholic from heretic, the legend has the legate answer, "Kill them all; God will know His own" — and thousands were slaughtered. The Inquisition was largely born of this campaign, to hunt out surviving heresy. The dictionary reads the Albigensian Crusade with sober eyes: a false gospel met not with the Word and the preaching of the cross, but with the literal sword of crusade — a grievous corruption of how Christ's church is to contend for the truth.
webster_summary: The thirteenth-century war (1209–1229) Rome and the French crown waged against the Cathar (Albigensian) heretics of southern France — suppressing a genuine dualist heresy by appalling slaughter, and giving rise to the Inquisition. A false gospel met by the sword rather than the Word.

Gave rise largely to the medieval Inquisition.

corruption_summary: The Albigensian Crusade is a double warning: the Cathar heresy itself corrupted the faith with dualism, and Rome's answer corrupted the church's warfare by taking up the carnal sword against error; the modern temptation is to make the Cathars innocent martyrs of free thought, which they were not.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet in the Albigensian Crusade. The Cathar error was a real heresy — a dualism that denied the goodness of creation, the true incarnation, and the resurrection of the body, and condemned marriage. It was not a purer Christianity but an old Gnostic poison, and the dictionary names it as such. Rome's corruption was the answer: not the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (Eph 6:17), but the literal sword of crusade, slaughtering whole cities and birthing the Inquisition. Christ's kingdom is not of this world, and His servants do not fight with steel (John 18:36).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition in its facts, but a romantic modern reading turns the Cathars into innocent victims of intolerance, martyrs of free thought. They were neither orthodox nor innocent of error. The principle to recover is twofold: heresy is real and must be opposed, but the weapons of the church's warfare are not carnal (2 Cor 10:4) — error is to be met in meekness, instructing those who oppose themselves, that God may grant repentance (2 Tim 2:25), not crushed by the crusader's blade.

etymology: From common (shared, public) + prayer; the English liturgy chiefly composed by Thomas Cranmer for the reformed Church of England.
biblical_def: The Book of Common Prayer is the English-language liturgy of the reformed Church of England, chiefly the work of Archbishop Thomas Cranmer, first issued in 1549, revised in 1552, and settled in the form of 1662 that endured for centuries. It was a fruit of the English Reformation: where the medieval church had prayed in Latin that the people could not understand, Cranmer gave England public worship in her own tongue, with the Scriptures read in course, the Psalms appointed through the month, and the great prayers framed in a noble English that shaped the language itself. Its theology, in the reformed editions, set forth justification by faith, the sufficiency of Christ's one sacrifice, and a Lord's Supper that turned away from the Mass toward a spiritual feeding by faith — though it kept an episcopal frame and forms of churchmanship the Puritans judged still half-reformed, and over which much later contention arose. This dictionary, holding a Baptist confession and the regulative principle, does not adopt a set liturgy as binding; yet it honors the Book of Common Prayer as a monument of the English Reformation, a vehicle that carried Scripture and reformed doctrine into the worship and memory of a whole people, and a treasury of biblical English prayer.
webster_summary: The English liturgy of the reformed Church of England, chiefly Cranmer's work (1549, 1552, settled 1662) — public worship in the people's tongue, with Scripture read in course and reformed doctrine in noble English. Honored as a monument of the English Reformation, though not adopted as binding by this Baptist dictionary.

corruption_summary: The Book of Common Prayer is corrupted from two sides: by the Anglo-Catholic revival that read the reformed liturgy back toward the Mass and priestly sacrifice it was framed to leave behind, and by a modern revision that has often diluted its biblical doctrine into vague and inclusive sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the Anglo-Catholic and Tractarian effort to undo the Reformation within the Prayer Book — reading Cranmer's reformed communion service as a sacrifice of the Mass, restoring the altar and the priesthood it was written to reject. The dictionary reads the reformed editions as their authors meant them: a turning from the Mass toward worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:24), with one finished sacrifice and a spiritual feeding by faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the historic text, which is fixed, but modern revisions have frequently softened its doctrine, trimming sin and judgment and inclusiveness of language at the cost of truth. The principle to recover is worship that joins spirit and understanding (1 Cor 14:15), letting the word of Christ dwell richly (Col 3:16), done decently and in order (1 Cor 14:40). The Book of Common Prayer at its best served that end; this Baptist dictionary honors it as a monument while holding that Scripture, not a fixed liturgy, governs the church's worship.

etymology: From Latin casus (a case), through the "cases of conscience"; the application of moral principles to particular cases — a good thing corrupted into a byword for sophistry.
biblical_def: Casuistry is, in its proper and original sense, the careful application of moral principles to particular cases of conscience — the work of helping a troubled believer discern his duty when the path is not plain. The Puritans excelled at it and called it "cases of conscience": William Perkins, William Ames, and Richard Baxter wrote whole treatises guiding the conscience through real questions of sin, duty, assurance, vocation, and the perplexities of the Christian life. Rightly done, casuistry is a pastoral necessity, for the law of God must be brought to bear on the actual circumstances men face, and the tender conscience needs faithful counsel. But the word fell into disgrace through its abuse, chiefly at the hands of the Jesuit moralists, whose probabilism and mental reservation taught men how to evade the plain commands of God by clever distinctions — finding a learned excuse for nearly any sin. So "casuistry" became a byword for sophistry, for arguing one's way around duty rather than to it. This dictionary holds the distinction: the Reformed and Puritan cases of conscience are a godly help, binding the conscience to God's law and easing the troubled soul; the corrupt casuistry that explains away the commandment is the conscience's enemy.
webster_summary: The application of moral principle to particular cases of conscience — a godly pastoral work in the Puritan "cases of conscience" (Perkins, Ames, Baxter), but corrupted by Jesuit moralists into a byword for sophistry that argues its way around God's plain commands.

corruption_summary: Casuistry is itself the name of a corruption when it is the art of evasion — the clever distinction that lets a man keep his sin with a clear conscience; the godly cases of conscience are its opposite, binding the conscience to the law of God rather than excusing it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that gave casuistry its bad name is the Jesuit art of evasion: probabilism, which let a man follow any "probable" opinion however lax; mental reservation, which let him deceive while technically not lying; and the multiplying of distinctions until the plain commandment had a hundred exceptions. This is the casuistry our Lord rebuked in the Pharisees, who strained at a gnat and swallowed a camel (Matt 23:24) — meticulous in trifles, evasive in the weighty matters of the law. The dictionary names this art of excuse as the enemy of the conscience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but the modern conscience tends toward the same evasion without the learning — finding reasons that a clear command does not really apply to me, in my case, today. The principle to recover is the good casuistry: bringing God's word, the lamp to the feet (Psa 119:105), to bear honestly on the actual case, that the senses may be exercised to discern good and evil (Heb 5:14), and remembering that whatsoever is not of faith is sin (Rom 14:23). The Puritan cases of conscience bind the soul to duty; corrupt casuistry looses it from duty. The dictionary keeps the one and rejects the other.

etymology: The town in Saxony, Germany, on the river Elbe; the cradle of the Lutheran Reformation, where Luther taught and posted his Ninety-Five Theses.
biblical_def: Wittenberg is the town in Saxony, on the river Elbe, where the Protestant Reformation was born. There, in 1502, the elector Frederick the Wise founded a new university, and to its faculty came an Augustinian monk named Martin Luther to teach the Scriptures. In Wittenberg Luther wrestled his way out of the terror of works-righteousness into the freedom of the gospel, finding in Romans that the just shall live by faith and that the righteousness of God is the gift He gives, not the standard He demands. On the eve of All Saints, the 31st of October 1517, Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses against indulgences on the door of the Castle Church at Wittenberg — the spark, in God's providence, that set Europe ablaze. From Wittenberg came the German Bible Luther translated, the preaching that recovered justification by faith, and the colleague Philip Melanchthon who systematized the new theology. The town that gave the world the Reformation's first cry is rightly called its cradle. This dictionary honors Wittenberg not for the timber of a church door but for what was recovered there: the gospel of grace, the open Bible, and the conscience bound only by the Word of God.
webster_summary: The town in Saxony where the Reformation was born — where Luther taught the Scriptures, found justification by faith in Romans, and posted his Ninety-Five Theses on the Castle Church door (31 October 1517). The cradle of the Reformation and of the recovered gospel.

corruption_summary: Wittenberg is corrupted when it is remembered as a place of mere historical interest — a tourist's church door, a national German legend — rather than as the place where the gospel of free grace was recovered for the whole church; the deeper danger is to keep the date and forget the doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that besets Wittenberg is sentimental forgetfulness: the church door becomes a relic, the Theses a museum piece, Luther a German hero, and the gospel that was recovered there quietly slips out of view. Even much of the church that bears Luther's name has long since let go of his message. But Wittenberg matters for one reason only: there a terrified monk found that the just shall live by faith (Rom 1:17), and that a sinner is justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ (Rom 3:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the history, but the temptation is to commemorate the event and neglect the truth. The principle to recover is the gospel itself: free grace, the open Bible, and Christian liberty — to stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made us free, and not be entangled again with the yoke of bondage (Gal 5:1). Wittenberg is honored rightly only when the doctrine recovered there is believed and preached, not merely visited.

etymology: From Geneva, the Swiss city of Calvin's reformation, + academy (Greek Akademeia, the school of Plato); the school Calvin founded in 1559 to train Reformed ministers.
biblical_def: The Geneva Academy was the school John Calvin founded at Geneva in 1559, near the end of his life, to train ministers and scholars for the Reformed churches — an engine that sent the recovered gospel across Europe. Geneva under Calvin had become, in John Knox's famous words, "the most perfect school of Christ that ever was in the earth since the days of the apostles." The Academy crowned that work. Under its first rector, Theodore Beza, Calvin's successor, it gathered students from France, the Netherlands, Scotland, England, Italy, and beyond, taught them the biblical languages and theology, and sent them home to plant and pastor churches, many of them to martyrdom. From the Geneva Academy went out the men who shaped the French Huguenot churches, the Dutch Reformed, and the Scottish Kirk; its model bore fruit in the later Reformed academies and seminaries. The school embodied a Reformation conviction: that the church is built by the preaching of the Word, and the Word is preached by men who must be carefully taught it. This dictionary honors the Geneva Academy as the seedbed of a generation of Reformed pastors, and as a pattern of the ministerial training the gospel requires — learning bent wholly to the service of the Word and the church.
webster_summary: The school Calvin founded at Geneva in 1559, under its first rector Theodore Beza, to train Reformed ministers — gathering students from across Europe and sending them home to plant and pastor churches. The seedbed of a generation of Reformed pastors and a pattern of ministerial training bent to the Word.

corruption_summary: The Geneva Academy's vision — rigorous training of ministers for the service of the Word — is corrupted today in two directions: by an anti-intellectual piety that despises learning, and by an academy that pursues scholarship cut loose from the church and the gospel it was meant to serve.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the despising of learning: the notion that an untaught zeal is enough, that the minister needs no careful grounding in the Scriptures, the languages, and sound doctrine. Calvin knew better. The priest's lips should keep knowledge, and men should seek the law at his mouth (Mal 2:7); the pastor must commit the faith to faithful men able to teach others (2 Tim 2:2). The Geneva Academy existed because the gospel requires taught teachers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the school, but its heirs — the seminaries and divinity schools — have too often drifted the other way, pursuing scholarship for its own sake, severed from the church, and even turning their learning against the faith they were founded to serve. The principle to recover is the Academy's own: learning wholly bent to the Word and the church, training pastors and teachers (Eph 4:11) who give attendance to reading, exhortation, and doctrine (1 Tim 4:13) for the sake of Christ's flock.

etymology: From the unbroken links of Romans 8:29–30 — foreknew, predestinated, called, justified, glorified; named the "golden chain" in the Reformed tradition, and the title of William Perkins's great work.
biblical_def: The golden chain of salvation is the Reformed name for the unbroken sequence of saving acts of God set forth in Romans 8:29–30: "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son... Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified." Five links, every one forged by God, and not a single one broken: foreknowledge (God's eternal setting of His love upon a people), predestination (His appointing them to be conformed to Christ), effectual calling (His drawing them in time by His Spirit), justification (His declaring them righteous in Christ by faith), and glorification (His final perfecting of them in glory, spoken of as already done, so sure is it). The whole chain is God's work from first to last; the sinner contributes nothing but the sin from which he is saved. The Puritan William Perkins took this passage as the title and theme of his great work, A Golden Chaine, mapping the order of salvation. This dictionary confesses the golden chain as the strong comfort of the believer: the God who began the good work will perform it (Phil 1:6), and not one link will fail, for all are held in His hand.
webster_summary: The Reformed name for the unbroken sequence of God's saving acts in Romans 8:29–30 — foreknew, predestinated, called, justified, glorified. Five links, every one God's work, none broken; the title of Perkins's great work and the strong comfort of the believer.
webster_full: GOLDEN CHAIN (OF SALVATION), noun phrase. The unbroken sequence of God's saving acts in Romans 8:29–30.
Five links: foreknowledge, predestination, effectual calling, justification, glorification.
Every link is God's own work; not one of them is broken.
Glorification is spoken of as already done, so sure is the believer's perfecting.
The title and theme of William Perkins's great Puritan work, A Golden Chaine.
scriptures: Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Phil 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
John 6:39
And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day.
corruption_summary: The golden chain is corrupted whenever a link is made to depend on man — election grounded in foreseen faith, calling resistible, justification mixed with works, or perseverance left to the believer's strength — for to break one link is to break the chain and rob the believer of his comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption of the golden chain is to slip a human link into the divine sequence. The Arminian reads "foreknew" as God foreseeing who would believe, making election hang on man's choice; others make the calling resistible, the justification dependent on works, or the final glorification uncertain. But Paul's chain has no human link: every verb has God for its subject, and the same number He foreknew He predestinated, called, justified, and glorified — the company does not shrink from one link to the next. To break the chain anywhere is to lose the gospel's comfort.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but the modern instinct, like the Arminian, wants salvation to rest somewhere on the self. The principle to recover is the unbreakable work of God: He who began the good work will perform it (Phil 1:6); of all the Father gave the Son, He will lose nothing (John 6:39). The golden chain is the believer's strong consolation — not that he holds God, but that God holds him, link by link, from eternity to glory.
roots_summary: From the unbroken links of Romans 8:29–30 (foreknew, predestinated, called, justified, glorified); the Reformed "golden chain" of salvation, all of it God's work.

etymology: Latin via (road) + Egnatia (after the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius who built it); the Roman highway across the Balkans by which Paul carried the gospel into Europe.
biblical_def: The Via Egnatia was the great Roman road that ran from the Adriatic coast across Macedonia and Thrace to Byzantium, the eastern continuation of the Appian Way and one of the chief highways of the empire — and along its course the apostle Paul carried the gospel into Europe. When Paul crossed from Asia into Macedonia after the vision of the man who cried "Come over and help us" (Acts 16:9), he landed at Neapolis and went up to Philippi, a city on the Via Egnatia, where Lydia was converted and the Philippian jailer was saved. The road then bore him westward to Amphipolis and Apollonia and to Thessalonica, and on toward Berea — the very cities to which his later epistles would be written. The Roman peace and the Roman roads, built for legions and trade, became in God's providence the arteries of the gospel; the empire that would persecute the church first paved the way for her message. This dictionary marks the Via Egnatia as a witness to that providence: the Lord of history ordered the roads of Caesar so that the good news of Christ might run swiftly from city to city, and the kingdoms of men served, all unknowing, the spread of the kingdom of God.
webster_summary: The great Roman highway across Macedonia and Thrace by which Paul carried the gospel into Europe — linking Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea. A witness that God ordered the roads and peace of Caesar's empire for the swift spread of the good news of Christ.
webster_full: VIA EGNATIA, proper noun. The Roman highway from the Adriatic across Macedonia and Thrace to Byzantium.
The eastern continuation of the Appian Way, one of the chief roads of the empire.
Linked Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica — cities of Paul's mission.
Paul carried the gospel into Europe along its course after the Macedonian vision (Acts 16:9).
A witness that God ordered Caesar's roads for the spread of the gospel.
scriptures: Acts 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Acts 17:1

Gal 4:4

how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no real redefinition; the danger is only a thin secular reading that sees in Paul's use of the Roman roads mere historical accident or clever strategy, and misses the providence of God who ordered the highways of empire for the running of His gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: The only corruption that threatens the Via Egnatia is the flattening of providence into accident. The secular historian sees a missionary who shrewdly used the imperial road network; and Paul did use it. But Scripture sees more: that when the fulness of time was come, God sent forth His Son (Gal 4:4), and that same God had prepared the stage — a common Greek tongue, a Roman peace, and Roman roads like the Via Egnatia — so that the gospel might run. The kingdoms of men served the kingdom of God all unaware.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over history. Paul did not stumble into Europe; he was called by a vision (Acts 16:9) and carried by a road Rome had built for other ends. How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace (Rom 10:15) — and how wonderful that God paved the road beneath those feet. The Via Egnatia preaches that the Lord of history bends the works of empires to the errand of His Son.

etymology: From the KJV's "strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Heb 11:13; 1 Pet 2:11); pilgrim from Latin peregrinus (a foreigner, one journeying through), stranger from Latin extraneus (one from without).
biblical_def: Pilgrim and stranger is the Scripture's name for what the believer is in this present world: a sojourner passing through a country not his home, a foreigner whose citizenship lies elsewhere. The patriarchs "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Heb 11:13), seeking a better country, that is, a heavenly, wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God. Peter takes up the same word, beseeching believers "as strangers and pilgrims" to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul (1 Pet 2:11). The Christian's home is not here. He holds the things of this life loosely, as a traveler holds the inn where he lodges a night, for his conversation — his citizenship — is in heaven (Phil 3:20), and he looks for the city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God (Heb 11:10). This is not a contempt for God's good creation but a refusal to settle down in a world under the curse as though it were the believer's lasting country. Bunyan made the whole of the Christian life a pilgrim's progress from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City. This dictionary confesses the pilgrim character of the Christian: he travels light, suffers as a sojourner, sets his affection on things above, and presses on toward home.
webster_summary: The Scripture's name for the believer in this world — a sojourner passing through a land not his home, whose citizenship is in heaven (Heb 11:13; 1 Pet 2:11; Phil 3:20). He holds this life loosely, sets his affection above, and presses on toward the city whose builder is God.
webster_full: PILGRIM AND STRANGER, noun phrase. The Scripture's name for the believer in this present world.
The patriarchs confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Heb 11:13).
Peter beseeches believers as strangers and pilgrims to abstain from fleshly lusts (1 Pet 2:11).
The Christian's citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:20); he seeks a better country.
Bunyan made the Christian life a pilgrim's progress toward the Celestial City.
scriptures: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.
Phil 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ.
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
corruption_summary: The pilgrim character of the Christian is corrupted by a worldliness that sinks its roots deep into this present age, treating earth as home and heaven as an afterthought; and by a false otherworldliness that despises God's good creation and the duties of this life, forgetting that the pilgrim still has a road to walk and work to do along it.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is to forget that we are pilgrims at all — to settle into the world, lay up treasure here, and live as though this life were the believer's lasting country. The prosperity preachers baptize this and call it blessing. But Peter calls believers strangers and pilgrims and bids them, as travelers, abstain from the fleshly lusts that war against the soul (1 Pet 2:11). The man who treats earth as home cannot help being entangled by it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but a second and opposite corruption must be marked: a sour otherworldliness that despises the good gifts of God and the honest duties of this life. The pilgrim is not a hermit who hates the road; he travels it faithfully, loving his neighbor, working his calling, using the world without abusing it. The principle to recover is the right balance: our citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:20), and we look for the city whose builder is God (Heb 11:10), yet we walk the pilgrim road with diligence and joy, holding this life loosely but not contemptuously, pressing on toward home.
roots_summary: From the KJV's "strangers and pilgrims" (Heb 11:13; 1 Pet 2:11); Latin peregrinus (a sojourner) and extraneus (one from without) — the believer's status in this world.
